solution.concept_anchor: Degrees of protection — 371A/371G strongest; others are administrative

statement_analysis.statement: Under Articles 371A (Nagaland) and 371G (Mizoram), Parliament is constitutionally barred from legislating on protected subjects unless the concerned state legislature passes a resolution — making these the strongest legislative shields under Article 371.
statement_analysis.reason: Articles 371A and 371G explicitly state that Acts of Parliament on specified subjects shall not apply to the state unless the state legislature so resolves — the only two Article 371 provisions with this mechanism.

statement_analysis.statement: Article 371B (Assam) and Article 371C (Manipur) offer a similar legislative shield — Parliament cannot legislate on hill or tribal area matters without those state legislatures' resolution.
statement_analysis.reason: Articles 371B and 371C do not contain any state-resolution requirement before Parliamentary legislation. They create committees and reporting mechanisms but do not bar Parliament from legislating on related subjects.

statement_analysis.statement: Article 371D (Andhra Pradesh) protections are implemented primarily through Presidential Orders ensuring equitable opportunities — Parliament retains full legislative competence and the protection is administrative in character.
statement_analysis.reason: Article 371D operates through Presidential Orders for equitable regional opportunities and establishes Administrative Tribunals — Parliament is not barred from legislating. The protection is executive/administrative, not a Parliamentary legislative bar.

statement_analysis.statement: Articles 371B and 371C protections are exclusively implemented through Presidential Orders identical in mechanism to Article 371D — there is no role for the Governor in their implementation.
statement_analysis.reason: Under 371C, the Governor has a specific and important role — including submitting an annual report to the President. The claim that the Governor plays 'no role' in 371B and 371C implementation is incorrect for 371C, and understates the President's role in 371B's committee constitution.

solution.strong_distractor: c — Students who correctly identify Statements 1 and 3 as correct but also incorrectly accept Statement 4 (not catching the Governor's role error in 371C) will select 'Only three.'
elimination_logic: Check Statement 1: 371A and 371G state-resolution requirement — strongest legislative shield — correct.
Check Statement 2: 371B and 371C do NOT have state-resolution requirements. Statement 2 is incorrect.
Check Statement 3: 371D operates through Presidential Orders; Parliament is not barred. Statement 3 is correct.
Check Statement 4: Governor of Manipur has an explicit role under 371C (annual report, oversight of Hill Areas). The 'no role for the Governor' claim is incorrect. Statement 4 is incorrect.
Statements 1 and 3 correct → 'Only two' → option (a).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The scope-extension trap in Statement 2 extends the 371A/371G resolution requirement to 371B and 371C — the most common misconception about NE state protections. Students who broadly know 'NE states have strong protections' assume the mechanism is the same across all of them. The trap in Statement 4 is the false claim that the Governor plays no role in 371C — the opposite is true.
solution.final_explanation:
The degree of legislative protection under Article 371 provisions follows a spectrum that UPSC tests precisely.

• Statement 1 — Correct: 371A and 371G are the only provisions with an explicit Parliamentary legislative bar requiring state-resolution — the strongest form of protection.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: 371B and 371C create committees and reporting mechanisms; they do not bar Parliamentary legislation through any state-resolution requirement.
• Statement 3 — Correct: 371D (Andhra Pradesh) works through Presidential Orders and Administrative Tribunals — Parliament retains full legislative competence. The protection is administrative, not a legislative bar.
• Statement 4 — Incorrect: The Governor of Manipur has a constitutionally explicit role under 371C — including the annual report to the President on Hill Area administration. The 'no role' claim is factually wrong.

Value Addition:
• The spectrum of Article 371 protection: Legislative bar (371A, 371G) > Governor's special role (371C, 371H, 371F) > Presidential Orders only (371D, 371B) > Structural (371I).
• No Article 371 provision other than 371A and 371G bars Parliamentary legislation on the protected subject.
• Post-Telangana bifurcation (2014), 371D's applicability to Telangana remains an unsettled question.

solution.concept_anchor: Asymmetric federalism — integration through accommodation
solution.strong_distractor: a — Students who know both that India practices asymmetric federalism AND that Articles 370/371 reflect this will assume R explains A without scrutinising whether the SC in 2023 used 'asymmetric federalism' as the reason for upholding abrogation.
elimination_logic: Step 1 — Is A correct? India's constitutional framework accommodates differential treatment of states based on historical, cultural, and strategic factors — evidenced by Articles 370, 371A-J, Fifth Schedule, Sixth Schedule, and special categories. This is correctly described as asymmetric federalism. A is correct.

Step 2 — Is R correct? The Supreme Court in its 2023 judgment on Article 370 did NOT hold that abrogation was constitutionally necessary because of asymmetric federalism. The Court upheld the abrogation based on the President's constitutional power and J&K's lack of internal sovereignty — not on the premise that uniform federalism is constitutionally required. R as stated is factually incorrect — it misrepresents the Court's actual reasoning.
Step 3 — Since R is factually incorrect, causal link is irrelevant.
A correct, R incorrect → option (c).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The reversed-causation trap constructs a plausible but false Reason. Students who know the 2023 SC judgment upholding abrogation may assume the Court endorsed a shift toward 'uniform federalism' — it did not. The Court's reasoning was grounded in J&K's lack of distinct sovereignty and the President's constitutional powers, not in a normative preference for uniform federalism. R is factually incorrect.
solution.final_explanation:
India's model of asymmetric federalism is a recurring UPSC theme — the 2023 SC judgment adds a layer of complexity.

• Assertion (A): Correct. India's federal structure is explicitly asymmetric — different states have different constitutional relationships with the Centre, based on their history, culture, and strategic importance. This is reflected in Articles 370, 371A-J, and the Schedule provisions.
• Reason (R): Incorrect. The Supreme Court in its 2023 judgment did NOT hold that abrogation of Article 370 was constitutionally necessary to achieve uniform federalism. The Court's majority upheld abrogation on the ground that J&K had no internal sovereignty distinct from other states post-accession, and that the President had the constitutional authority to exercise Article 370(3) powers through the mechanism adopted. Normative uniform federalism was NOT the Court's rationale.

Value Addition:
• The Constituent Assembly debate on Article 370 explicitly acknowledged asymmetric accommodation as a tool of national integration.
• Scholars describe India's model as 'holding together' federalism — as opposed to 'coming together' federalism (like the USA).
• Post-2019, the debate on whether India is moving toward symmetric federalism continues — but the SC 2023 judgment does not constitutionally mandate it.

solution.concept_anchor: Chronological order — 371D, 371E, 371F, 371J insertion years
solution.strong_distractor: b — Students who know 371F relates to Sikkim (merged 1975) and 371J is recent (2012) but are unsure whether 371D/371E preceded 371F or followed it will choose (b), reversing 371D/371E and 371F.
elimination_logic: Identify 371D/371E insertion: the 32nd Constitutional Amendment Act (1973) inserted Articles 371D and 371E for Andhra Pradesh.
Identify 371F insertion: the 36th Constitutional Amendment Act (1975) inserted Article 371F for Sikkim following its merger.
Identify 371J insertion: the 105th Constitutional Amendment Act (2012) inserted Article 371J for Karnataka — the most recent.
Identify 371A insertion: the 13th Constitutional Amendment Act (1962) inserted Article 371A when Nagaland became a state.
Correct chronological order by insertion year: 371A (1962) → 371D/371E (1973) → 371F (1975) → 371J (2012) → option (c).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The temporal-swap trap works by making students confuse the Andhra Pradesh provisions (371D/371E — 1973) with the Sikkim provision (371F — 1975). Both happened in the 1970s in close succession, making the sequence easily reversible. Additionally, students who know Nagaland became a state in 1963 may misplace 371A at 1963 rather than 1962 (the amendment year).
solution.final_explanation:
Sequencing Article 371 sub-articles by year of insertion reveals the evolution of India's asymmetric federal accommodation.

Correct sequence:
1. Article 371A (1962) — 13th Constitutional Amendment; Nagaland statehood in 1963.
2. Articles 371D and 371E (1973) — 32nd Constitutional Amendment; special provisions for Andhra Pradesh.
3. Article 371F (1975) — 36th Constitutional Amendment; Sikkim's merger as India's 22nd state.
4. Article 371J (2012) — 105th Constitutional Amendment; special provision for Hyderabad-Karnataka (Karnataka).

Wrong options swap 371D/371E and 371F, or misplace 371J as predating Sikkim's provisions.

Value Addition:
• Nagaland became a state in 1963 — one year after the 13th Amendment inserted 371A in 1962.
• Andhra Pradesh's 32nd Amendment provisions (371D/371E) predate Sikkim's merger by two years.
• 371J (2012) is the most recent — spanning 50 years of Article 371 expansion from 1962 to 2012.

solution.concept_anchor: Sixth Schedule — creates ADCs with legislative/judicial/executive powers
solution.strong_distractor: d — Students who know the Sixth Schedule applies to NE states and involves tribal protections may conflate it with the targeted land-protection provisions of Articles 371A/371G, selecting (d) which describes those provisions rather than the Sixth Schedule.
elimination_logic: Eliminate (a): The Sixth Schedule does not require state legislature resolutions before Parliament legislates — that is the mechanism under 371A and 371G. The Sixth Schedule creates bodies with their own legislative power.
Eliminate (c): The Sixth Schedule applies to Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura, and Mizoram — Nagaland and Arunachal Pradesh are NOT under the Sixth Schedule.

Eliminate (d): The description of protecting 'land ownership and customary law from Parliamentary override through state-resolution mechanisms' describes Articles 371A and 371G, not the Sixth Schedule.

Confirm (b): The Sixth Schedule creates Autonomous District Councils with powers to legislate on specified tribal matters, run district courts, and administer tribal affairs — constituting structural autonomy through sub-state governance bodies.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The conflation trap merges the Sixth Schedule's structural autonomy (ADC creation) with Article 371's targeted protections. Students who associate both with 'tribal protection in NE India' may not distinguish that the Sixth Schedule creates actual governance bodies while Article 371 provisions are targeted protections without creating new governmental structures (for the most part).
solution.final_explanation:
The Sixth Schedule is one of the Constitution's most powerful instruments of tribal governance — qualitatively different from Article 371 protections.

• Option (a) — Incorrect: The Sixth Schedule does not require state legislature resolutions before Parliamentary legislation. The 371A/371G mechanism is separate.
• Option (b) — Correct: The Sixth Schedule creates Autonomous District Councils (ADCs) with legislative, executive, and judicial powers over specified tribal matters — a structural sub-state governance framework.
• Option (c) — Incorrect: The Sixth Schedule covers Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura, and Mizoram. Nagaland and Arunachal Pradesh are NOT Sixth Schedule states — Nagaland has its own tribal law framework under Article 371A.
• Option (d) — Incorrect: This describes Articles 371A and 371G, not the Sixth Schedule.

Value Addition:
• The Bodoland Territorial Council (Assam) and Karbi Anglong ADC are examples of Sixth Schedule bodies.
• ADCs can make laws on 21 specific subjects listed in the Sixth Schedule.
• The Sixth Schedule's judicial powers allow ADCs to try certain civil and criminal cases among tribals.

solution.concept_anchor: Mizo Accord 1986 — genesis of Article 371G

statement_analysis.statement: Article 371G was inserted into the Constitution following the Mizo Accord of 1986, which ended the Mizo insurgency and provided for Mizoram's elevation from a Union Territory to a full state.
statement_analysis.reason: The Mizo Accord of 1986 between the Government of India and the Mizo National Front (Laldenga) was the political basis for Mizoram's statehood and the constitutional protections under Article 371G — directly parallel to how the 16-Point Agreement generated Article 371A for Nagaland.

statement_analysis.statement: Unlike Article 371A (Nagaland), Article 371G (Mizoram) does NOT require a Mizoram Legislative Assembly resolution before Parliamentary legislation on protected subjects applies — the protection operates automatically through Presidential Orders.
statement_analysis.reason: Article 371G contains the same state-resolution requirement as Article 371A — Parliament's legislation on Mizo customary law, land ownership, transfer, and village administration shall not apply unless the Mizoram Legislative Assembly so resolves. The claim that it operates through Presidential Orders without a resolution requirement is factually wrong.

solution.strong_distractor: a — Students who broadly know both Mizoram's Accord history and 371G's protective nature may accept both statements as correct, failing to catch the false claim in Statement 2 that the mechanism is through Presidential Orders (not resolution).
elimination_logic: Evaluate Statement 1: Mizo Accord 1986 + Mizoram's statehood + Article 371G insertion — factually accurate. Statement 1 is correct.

Evaluate Statement 2: The claim that 371G does NOT require a state resolution and operates through Presidential Orders is factually wrong. 371G explicitly mirrors 371A's resolution requirement. Statement 2 is incorrect.
Statement 1 correct, Statement 2 incorrect → option (d).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The entity-swap trap substitutes the Presidential Order mechanism (used in 371D and 371B) for the resolution requirement that correctly characterises both 371A and 371G. Students who know 371A requires a resolution but are uncertain whether 371G is identical or different may accept Statement 2's false claim — especially since it attributes a mechanism that does exist elsewhere under Article 371 (Presidential Orders).
solution.final_explanation:
The Mizo Accord of 1986 and Article 371G form one of the most important political-constitutional couplings in Indian history.

• Statement 1 — Correct: The Mizo Accord (1986) ended two decades of insurgency. Under the Accord, Mizoram was elevated from a UT to a full state, and Article 371G was inserted to honour the commitment to protect Mizo customary practices and land rights — directly paralleling how the 16-Point Agreement generated Article 371A for Nagaland.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: Article 371G contains an explicit state-resolution requirement, identical in structure to Article 371A. Parliament cannot apply its legislation on protected subjects (Mizo customary law, land ownership, village administration) without the Mizoram Legislative Assembly's resolution. Presidential Orders are NOT the mechanism — the resolution requirement is.

Value Addition:
• Laldenga, the Mizo National Front leader, became Mizoram's first Chief Minister after the Accord.
• Mizoram became a state on February 20, 1987.
• The 1986 Accord is considered one of India's most successful insurgency-resolution agreements — a model studied alongside the Punjab Accord and Assam Accord of the same period.

solution.concept_anchor: SC 2023 — sovereignty trap and use of Article 356 Proclamation

statement_analysis.statement: The Supreme Court in its 2023 judgment affirmed that J&K had surrendered all sovereignty upon signing the Instrument of Accession — it had no internal sovereignty distinct from other Indian states, and Article 370's special status was not a recognition of residual sovereignty.
statement_analysis.reason: This is the central sovereignty holding of the 2023 judgment. The Court explicitly rejected the argument that J&K retained a special sovereign status by virtue of the Instrument of Accession, holding that accession was complete and absolute.

statement_analysis.statement: The Supreme Court validated the use of the Article 356 Proclamation (President's Rule) as a constitutional mechanism to obtain the concurrence of the J&K Legislature through Parliament — thereby legitimising the Government's approach in abrogating Article 370.
statement_analysis.reason: The majority upheld this step in the abrogation process — holding that Parliament, exercising J&K state legislature functions during President's Rule, could provide the concurrence required under Article 370(3) as modified by CO 272.

statement_analysis.statement: The Supreme Court ordered that J&K must immediately be restored to full statehood before elections could be held, and set a deadline of December 31, 2023 for both events.
statement_analysis.reason: The Court directed that elections be held by September 30, 2024 and endorsed the restoration of statehood as early as possible — but did NOT require statehood restoration before elections, nor did it set December 31, 2023 as the deadline.

solution.strong_distractor: d — Students who accept Statements 1 and 2 as correct but also incorrectly believe Statement 3 is correct (conflating the election deadline with a statehood-before-election requirement) will choose (d).
elimination_logic: Confirm Statement 1: The sovereignty holding — J&K had no internal sovereignty post-accession — is the SC's definitive position. Statement 1 is correct.
Confirm Statement 2: The Court validated Article 356's use in the abrogation process — the majority upheld Parliament acting as J&K's legislature to provide concurrence. Statement 2 is correct.
Examine Statement 3: The Court set September 30, 2024 (not December 31, 2023) for elections and did NOT require statehood restoration before elections. Statement 3 is incorrect.
Statements 1 and 2 correct → option (b).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The partial-truth trap in Statement 3 uses a plausible date (December 31, 2023 — within 2023 itself) and a plausible sequence (statehood before elections) that sound like what the SC might have ordered. The actual deadline was September 30, 2024 for elections — and statehood restoration was directed 'at the earliest,' not as a precondition for elections.
solution.final_explanation:
The 2023 SC judgment is one of the most consequential constitutional rulings of recent years — examining it at the level of specific holdings is essential for Prelims.

• Statement 1 — Correct: The sovereignty ruling is the judgment's analytical core — J&K had no distinct internal sovereignty. The Instrument of Accession effected complete integration; Article 370 was an accommodation, not a recognition of separate sovereignty.
• Statement 2 — Correct: The Court upheld the use of Article 356 as part of the abrogation sequence. Parliament, acting as J&K's legislature during President's Rule, validly provided the concurrence required under the modified Article 370(3).
• Statement 3 — Incorrect: Two errors are embedded. First, the election deadline was September 30, 2024 — not December 31, 2023. Second, the Court directed restoration of statehood 'as early as possible' but did NOT make statehood a precondition for elections.

Value Addition:
• The 5-judge Constitution Bench was led by CJI D.Y. Chandrachud.
• The judgment referenced the basic structure doctrine but held that J&K's special status was not part of the Constitution's basic structure.
• The Delimitation Commission completed J&K's constituency delimitation before the elections — another UPSC-relevant process.

• Goa's statehood (1987) preceded the insertion of Article 371I.
• Nagaland's 16-Point Agreement also committed the Government to a ceasefire and eventual political settlement — the constitutional protection was one element of a broader compact.

solution.concept_anchor: Article 371H — Governor's individual judgement overrides Article 163
solution.strong_distractor: b — Students who know both facts (371H discretion and Article 163 as the general rule) may not pause to verify whether R actually explains A — they may assume R is merely a correlating fact rather than the direct causal explanation.
elimination_logic: Step 1 — Is A correct? Under Article 371H, the Governor of Arunachal Pradesh exercises individual judgement specifically on law and order matters — not bound by the CoM's advice on this subject. This is factually accurate.

Step 2 — Is R correct? Article 163 lays down the general constitutional rule: Governors act on the advice of the CoM except where the Constitution requires them to act in their individual judgement. This is factually accurate.

Step 3 — Does R causally explain A? Yes — Article 371H is a specific constitutional provision that carves out an exception to the general rule in Article 163. The Governor of Arunachal Pradesh acts in individual judgement on law and order because Article 371H explicitly authorises this deviation from the Article 163 norm. R is the correct causal explanation of A.
Both A and R correct, R explains A → option (a).
solution.final_explanation:
Article 371H and Article 163 interact in a foundational principal-exception relationship.

• Assertion (A): Correct. Article 371H confers on the Governor of Arunachal Pradesh the explicit authority to act in individual judgement on law and order — without being bound by the CoM's advice on this specific subject. This is one of the very few explicit constitutional overrides of the CoM-advice rule.
• Reason (R): Correct. Article 163 establishes the general rule — Governors act on CoM advice except where the Constitution specifically requires individual judgement. Article 371H is precisely such a constitutionally mandated exception.
• Causal link: R directly explains A. The Governor of Arunachal Pradesh has individual discretion on law and order because Article 371H is a named constitutional exception to Article 163's general rule — R is the correct explanation.

Value Addition:
• Other constitutional provisions where Governors have individual judgement: summoning/dissolving legislature, seeking reports, reserving Bills for Presidential assent — but these are general; 371H is specific to law and order.
• The 2016 Arunachal Pradesh crisis tested 371H's limits — the SC intervened on different constitutional grounds (floor of the House, etc.).
• Article 163(2) bars courts from inquiring whether any matter falls within or outside the Governor's individual judgement — a significant limitation on judicial review.

solution.concept_anchor: Article 3 — consultation not consent; UT without legislature (Ladakh)

statement_analysis.statement: The J&K Reorganisation Act 2019, passed under Article 3, required the consent of the J&K Legislature before Parliament could proceed with the bifurcation — a requirement that was deemed satisfied through Parliament's own resolution during President's Rule.
statement_analysis.reason: Article 3 requires only 'consultation' (referral for views), NOT 'consent.' The state legislature's views are sought but not binding. Describing Parliament's role as satisfying a 'consent' requirement mischaracterises the constitutional position.

statement_analysis.statement: Ladakh, as a Union Territory without a legislature, is constitutionally comparable to Chandigarh and Lakshadweep — all three are UTs where Parliament directly legislates and there is no elected territorial legislature.
statement_analysis.reason: This statement is factually accurate — Ladakh, Chandigarh, and Lakshadweep are all UTs without their own legislatures, governed directly through Parliament and administered by a Lieutenant Governor. It does NOT qualify as 'incorrect.'

statement_analysis.statement: Following the bifurcation of Andhra Pradesh in 2014 (creating Telangana), the Article 371D protections automatically extended to all regions of Telangana in full — including the establishment of new Administrative Tribunals for service matters in Telangana.
statement_analysis.reason: The automatic extension of Article 371D protections to Telangana is contested — the provision was designed for Andhra Pradesh's regions, and its applicability to Telangana (a new state) requires fresh Presidential Orders. New Administrative Tribunals were not automatically created. The claim of 'automatic full extension' is legally inaccurate.

solution.strong_distractor: b — Students who catch Statement 1's 'consent vs. consultation' error but are unsure about Statement 3's Telangana applicability question may choose (b) — identifying only Statement 1 as incorrect.
elimination_logic: Evaluate Statement 1: Article 3 requires 'consultation,' not 'consent.' Using 'consent' mischaracterises the constitutional requirement. Statement 1 is NOT correct.
Evaluate Statement 2: Ladakh, Chandigarh, and Lakshadweep are all correctly identified as UTs without their own legislatures. Statement 2 is factually correct — does not qualify as 'not correct.'

Evaluate Statement 3: Article 371D's extension to Telangana is not automatic — it requires fresh Presidential Orders. The 'automatic full extension' claim is legally incorrect. Statement 3 is NOT correct.
Statements 1 and 3 are NOT correct → option (d).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The scope-extension trap in Statement 1 elevates 'consultation' to 'consent' — the most tested distinction in Article 3 questions. Statement 3's trap is the implicit claim that constitutional provisions designed for a state automatically apply to a successor state upon bifurcation — they generally require fresh Presidential Orders or legislative action to operationalise in the new state.
solution.final_explanation:
Both Article 3's bifurcation procedure and the post-bifurcation applicability of special provisions are UPSC-critical distinctions.

• Statement 1 — Incorrect: Article 3 requires only referral for the state legislature's views — consultation, not consent. Parliament is not bound by the state legislature's views. The substitution of 'consent' for 'consultation' is a critical scope-extension error.
• Statement 2 — Correct: Ladakh (UT without legislature), Chandigarh (UT without legislature), and Lakshadweep (UT without legislature) are correctly classified together. Parliament directly legislates for these territories.
• Statement 3 — Incorrect: Article 371D's Presidential Orders for equitable opportunities and Administrative Tribunals were designed for Andhra Pradesh's specific regions. Following Telangana's creation in 2014, fresh Presidential Orders are needed to operationalise these protections in Telangana — the extension is not automatic.

Value Addition:
• UTs with legislatures: Delhi (NCT), Puducherry, J&K — they have their own elected assemblies.
• UTs without legislatures are governed under the Union Territories Act, 1963.
• The Andhra Pradesh Reorganisation Act 2014 left the 371D applicability to Telangana as an unresolved question — a live constitutional issue.

solution.concept_anchor: Fifth and Sixth Schedule land protections coexist with 371A/371G independently
solution.strong_distractor: b — Students who know the Sixth Schedule applies to some NE states and also protects tribal land may incorrectly conclude that 371A/371G derive their land protection authority from or are subordinate to the Sixth Schedule.
elimination_logic: Eliminate (a): The ILP (Bengal Eastern Frontier Regulation 1873) is a statutory instrument — not the constitutional source of 371A/371G land protections. The two coexist but are legally independent.

Eliminate (b): The Sixth Schedule creates ADCs with powers over land use, but 371A and 371G are independent constitutional provisions — they neither derive from nor are subordinate to the Sixth Schedule.

Eliminate (d): Fundamental Rights under Part III do not provide land protection mechanisms for specific states; the specific protections under 371A/371G are Part XXI provisions — they are the operative mechanisms.

Confirm (c): The Fifth and Sixth Schedule land protection mechanisms exist alongside 371A/371G independently — neither framework is derivative of the other; they serve complementary but distinct constitutional purposes.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The conflation trap merges the Sixth Schedule's land use powers with the 371A/371G land ownership protections, leading students to assume one derives from or supplements the other. In fact, Nagaland is NOT under the Sixth Schedule while having strong 371A protections — confirming they are entirely independent frameworks.
solution.final_explanation:
The relationship between Article 371A/371G land protections and the Fifth/Sixth Schedule frameworks is an important comparative constitutional question.

• Option (a) — Incorrect: The ILP (Bengal Eastern Frontier Regulation 1873) is a statutory entry-restriction mechanism — not the constitutional source of land ownership protections under 371A/371G.
• Option (b) — Incorrect: The Sixth Schedule creates ADCs with land-use regulatory powers, but 371A and 371G are independent Part XXI provisions. They do not derive authority from the Sixth Schedule — Nagaland has 371A but is NOT a Sixth Schedule state.
• Option (c) — Correct: The Fifth Schedule (for central/peninsular tribal areas) and Sixth Schedule (for NE tribal areas) protection mechanisms coexist alongside 371A/371G as legally independent frameworks — neither is derivative of the other.
• Option (d) — Incorrect: Fundamental Rights in Part III do not provide the specific land protection mechanism applicable to Nagaland or Mizoram — 371A/371G are the operative constitutional instruments.

Value Addition:
• Nagaland: 371A applies; Sixth Schedule does NOT apply — confirming the two are independent.
• Mizoram: 371G applies AND it has Sixth Schedule ADCs — confirming they coexist without hierarchy.
• The Fifth Schedule applies to states like Jharkhand, Odisha, and Chhattisgarh — not the NE states covered by 371A/371G.
